newsitem.title: UK: Blair win puts pressure on IRA for truce - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Blair win puts pressure on IRA for truce - analysts.

text.p: Tony Blair's sweeping British election victory has put strong pressure on IRA guerrillas to call a truce to revive Northern Ireland's floundering peace process, political analysts said on Friday.

Political commentators in the troubled province said Blair's landslide win would remove a crucial factor that Sinn Fein blamed for its distrust of outgoing Prime Minister John Major -- a dependence in his final months on the votes of pro-British Protestant legislators from Northern Ireland.

"Blair has such a thumping majority that the pressure must now be on for Sinn Fein to convince the IRA to call a convincing ceasefire," David Davin-Power, Northern Ireland editor of the Irish broadcasting network RTE, told Reuters.

In the wake of Labour's historic victory, there was no word from the underground Irish Republican Army, fighting to end British rule. But during a bitterly fought campaign for seats in Northern Ireland, its Sinn Fein wing said the election could "change the course of Irish history".

Mo Mowlam, tipped to become the British minister with the task of steering the province out of the current stalemate, said Sinn Fein would not be allowed into talks until its IRA ally forsook violence. "They know the conditions...," she said.

During the campaign Mowlam promised to continue the broad bi-partisan approach that Labour had followed with the outgoing Conservatives, but said that if appointed she would implement measures that she hopes will ease tension between minority Irish Catholics and majority pro-British Protestants.

Sinn Fein, which demands "confidence building" measures such as police reform and revamped laws to eradicate job discrimination against Catholics, said after Labour's win that it would be flexible in trying to rebuild the peace process.
Sinn Fein sources say they need a firm date for admission to negotiations to persuade the IRA to call a truce.

But political observers said although Blair would not put himself in a position of being seen to be "soft on terrorism", republicans might see his strong position in government as radically improving the political climate.
"The atmospherics will be better," said one commentator.

As parties across the troubled province pledged to work with Blair to kick-start deadlocked peace efforts, political experts said he would not change Britain's approach to Northern Ireland but his win would exert pressure on the guerrillas to "to seize the moment" and call a ceasefire to win a seat in talks.

"The logic of everything that Sinn Fein has said recently points towards a new ceasefire announced quite quickly to see whether they can take advantage of the new government and to determine whether its new circumstances are more propitious for what they want," Paul Bew, politics professor at Queen's University, Belfast, told Reuters.
Ahead of the declaration of results for Northern Ireland's 18 seats in the British parliament, in which Sinn Fein hoped to win at least two, analyst Henry Patterson was optimistic.

"I think there is going to be a ceasefire quite soon, but it will probably depend on how they (Sinn Fein) do today. If they do quite well it will strengthen the hand of the pro-ceasefire lobby (amomg republicans)," said Patterson, a politics professor at the University of Ulster in Belfast.

Northern Ireland's peace drive has languished in the shadow of a wave of IRA violence for more than a year. Bombs disrupted transport during electioneering on the British mainland but the IRA have not struck in Northern Ireland since April 10.

Mark Simpson, political correspondent of the Belfast Telegraph newspaper, said any IRA truce plan could be torpedoed by the province's underlying volatility, such as the potential for street trouble over contentious summer Protestant parades.

"There is still a debate going on within the Republican Movement (Sinn Fein and the IRA), and the option has been left open of another ceasefire, very clearly by the fact that they have not gone back to full-scale violence. They will be hammering down Mo Mowlam's door when she takes office, demanding talks," he said.
